_note: English texts for data/examples/index.json (event and 'why it is famous'). Moves cited in English notation; notMoves = cited moves that are not moves of the game (historical references).

anderssen-kieseritzky-1851.famous: "The Immortal Game": Anderssen gives up both rooks, a bishop and finally the queen (22.Qf6+) and mates with the minor pieces.

anderssen-dufresne-1852.famous: "The Evergreen Game": the queen sacrifice 21.Qxd7+ opens the way to a mate by the bishops.

morphy-opera-1858.black: Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard
morphy-opera-1858.famous: "The Opera Game": Morphy develops all his pieces, sacrifices the queen with 16.Qb8+ and mates with the rook.

steinitz-bardeleben-1895.famous: Brilliancy prize at Hastings: after 22.Rxe7+ the white rook gives check after check on the seventh rank, and von Bardeleben leaves the hall without waiting for the mate.

rotlewi-rubinstein-1907.famous: "Rubinstein's Immortal": a chain of sacrifices starting with 22...Rxc3 and ending with 25...Rh3.

reti-tartakower-1910.famous: One of the most famous miniatures: Réti sacrifices the queen with 9.Qd8+ and finishes with a double check.

capablanca-marshall-1918.famous: Marshall unveils the gambit 8...d5 in the Ruy Lopez, today called the Marshall Attack; Capablanca repels the attack and wins.

botvinnik-capablanca-1938.famous: The future champion beats the former champion: 30.Ba3 starts a combination in which White also sacrifices the queen.

byrne-fischer-1956.famous: "The Game of the Century": Fischer, aged 13, gives up the queen with 17...Be6 and wins with the minor pieces.

fischer-spassky-1972-6.famous: Fischer, who almost always opened 1.e4, plays 1.c4 and wins; Spassky himself is said to have applauded.

karpov-kasparov-1985-16.famous: The black knight on d3 (16...Nd3) paralyses White for the whole game: Kasparov considered it the finest game of the match that made him champion.

deepblue-kasparov-1997-6.event: Man vs machine match, New York, game 6
deepblue-kasparov-1997-6.famous: With the sacrifice 8.Nxe6 Deep Blue wins in 19 moves and closes the match: the first time a computer beat the world champion in a match.

kasparov-topalov-1999.famous: "Kasparov's Immortal": 24.Rxd4 starts a king hunt that drives the black king to a3 and beyond.

polgar-kasparov-2002.event: Russia vs Rest of the World (rapid), Moscow
polgar-kasparov-2002.famous: The strongest female player of all time beats Kasparov, the world number one: her only win against him, in a rapid game.

carlsen-ernst-2004.event: Wijk aan Zee tournament, group C
carlsen-ernst-2004.famous: Carlsen is 13: with the sacrifices 18.Ng6 and 21.Bxh6 he opens up the black king and wins the game that made him known to the world.

aronian-anand-2013.famous: Anand, with Black, sacrifices several pieces and wins in 23 moves: he himself counts it among the best games of his life.

carlsen-anand-2013-5.famous: Carlsen's first win in the title match: from a small advantage he reaches an endgame and wins it patiently.

anand-carlsen-2013-9.famous: Anand attacks on the kingside but goes wrong at the critical moment: with this win Carlsen moves within a step of the title.

carlsen-karjakin-2016-10.event: World Championship match, New York, game 10
carlsen-karjakin-2016-10.famous: One point down, Carlsen levels the match by winning a long endgame: a typical example of his "grinding" style.

carlsen-karjakin-2016-rapid4.event: World Championship match, New York, rapid tiebreak 4
carlsen-karjakin-2016-rapid4.famous: Carlsen keeps the title, finishing the tiebreak with the queen sacrifice 50.Qh6+.

carlsen-nepomniachtchi-2021-6.famous: 136 moves: the longest game in the history of world championship matches. Carlsen wins it and the match turns.
